items.title: Bill Goodwin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 28, 2025
items.q: I first met Bobby Hutcherson when Terry Trotter, the pianist, took me over to Bobby’s house to play with Bobby and him and Herbie Lewis the bass player.

ctx.x: Yeah. I first met Bobby Hutcherson when Terry Trotter, the pianist, took me over to Bobby’s house to play with Bobby and him and Herbie Lewis the bass player. And they were a year older than me. And the first thing Bobby said to me after, “Do you have any marijuana” was, “Can you play fast?” I said, “I don’t know, let’s find out.” So they put “From This Moment on” way, way up. And, you know, I guess I did okay. I really didn’t

know how to play the drums. I had no technique at all, but I could hear and I could follow music and I could play music in other words, I just didn’t have a solid technique on the drums or any technique on the drums.

items.title: Bobby Hutcherson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Her brother, Bill Goodwin, the drummer

ctx.x: Yeah, right. See, at the same time, you’re on-the-job training, plus talking to people as you go into those jam sessions, and watching how – you listen to a lot of voicings. There’s a lot of voicings that Sonny Clark was playing and Gerald Wiggins and these guys. What is that? What have you got there in your hand? Why is sound causing? Oh look. There’s just that third, and there’s that seventh. Look at that. Here’s all this other stuff over here. All of a sudden I said wow.

Then all of a sudden I said – I used to try to play exactly like John Coltrane, after I learned that I couldn’t play like Milt Jackson. I tried Milt Jackson for a while, but that just – I just couldn’t. After a while I realized. I said, that’s Milt’s cookies. What are you doing trying to mess with Milt Jackson? Milt Jackson had – plus Milt Jackson was so fluid. I just – leave that alone. That belongs to him. How can you do that? So then I started listening a lot to John Coltrane, because it was so big at the…
